The session begins.

The Trade Way ends in noise. Wyrm's Crossing swallows the road whole: a bridge so crowded with shops, stalls and bodies that the river shows only in gaps between the planks. It smells of tar, fried fish and too many people. Across the water the walls of Baldur's Gate catch the last of the light, and lamplighters work their way along the parapet.

At the bridge's mouth the crowd thickens into a line. A Flaming Fist sergeant in a scorched-red tabard stops each cart and each stranger, looks them over and asks the same flat questions: name, business, how long. Refugees with bundles wait without complaint. A pair of sellswords argue the toll.

To the left, under a swinging lantern, a tiefling has turned a barrel into a card table. "One hand, friend, one hand before the gate," he calls, shuffling with long, quick fingers. Three players hunch over their cards. A fourth stool stands empty, and on it lies a coin, face up. Tymora's face. The lantern light catches it. No one at the table looks at it, and no one takes it.

The cat stops at James's boot and looks at the barrel.

The line shuffles a step forward. The sergeant's eyes have already found the tall stranger in the Tethyrian cloak.

*(Aside: the sergeant at the checkpoint is a woman, Sergeant Marla Ostrand, so I'll read "he" as a slip. James hasn't chosen anything yet, so the world just takes one step toward him.)*

The sergeant doesn't wait for the line to bring him to her. She steps out from beside the toll-post, leaving a private to handle a fishwife's handcart. She covers the few paces of plank between them with her thumb hooked in her belt. Up close she's older than she looked from the back of the line: soot in the creases of her tabard, a long day in the set of her jaw. Her eyes go to the grey cloak, then to the rod, then to the coin on its cord at his throat. They stay on the coin a moment longer than on the rest.

"You. Cloak." Her voice is flat. "Name. Business in the Gate. How long."

Behind her, Vesk lets the cards ripple from one hand to the other and smiles at nobody in particular. One of his three players lays a bad hand down and swears quietly.

Marla follows James's eyes, or the cat's, to the barrel and the empty stool with the coin on it. Something tightens around her mouth.

"You want to lose your money, that's your own business. After you've cleared my post." She jerks her chin at the stool without looking at it again. "And not on that seat."

She waits. The private at the toll-post has stopped pretending to count the fishwife's coppers.

"Name," she says again.

Marla hears him out without nodding. Her eyes go once more to the coin at his throat, then back to his face. The soldier's voice has registered with her. Her shoulders don't loosen, but she stops reaching for the next question as quickly as before.

"Neither," she says.

Behind her the private takes the fishwife's coppers at last, and the handcart rattles off onto the bridge.

"Bridge custom. A coin on an empty seat stays where it lies." She keeps her eyes on James, not on the barrel. "Whoever picks it up takes the seat. And whatever comes with the seat."

She doesn't say what that is.

At the barrel Vesk laughs, a little too loudly. "River talk, sergeant, old wives on the planks, nothing more. The man's welcome to sit anywhere, the coin's just — it's just luck, that's all, somebody's dropped luck—" He's dealing as he talks. One card slides off the edge of the barrelhead, and he catches it before it hits the boards.

Marla doesn't turn round. The cat does. It watches the card, then Vesk's hands, and its tail stops moving.

"Work and lodgings," Marla repeats, as if she's writing it down somewhere behind her eyes. Her gaze drops to the grey wool on his shoulders, the worn regimental cut, the faded braid at the collar. "That's a Tethyrian cloak. Zaranda's colours."

She hooks her thumb back into her belt.

"Whose company did you serve with, Worgen? And can you show me something that says so?"

Marla takes the slip in two fingers and turns it to catch the lantern. She reads it all the way through: the name, the unit, the seal. Her thumb rests on the wax and runs once along the edge where the impression has gone soft with years of folding. It's real, and she can see that. She doesn't pretend otherwise.

"Sixth Foot. Scouts." She folds it back along its old creases and hands it over. "Good order's more than most of the sellswords on this bridge can show."

The private at the toll-post holds out a palm for the walking fare. Marla shakes her head once without turning, and the hand drops.

"You're cleared, Worgen." She says the name the way she'd file it. "Lodgings in the Lower City cost more than out here and are worth it. The gate shuts at full dark. You've got the time if you don't stop."

She's already looking past him at the next cart in the line. Then her eyes go back, very briefly, to the coin at his throat, and from that to the stool. Whatever she's thinking, she keeps it to herself and steps back to the post.

The planks open in front of him. The bridge runs on through the stalls toward the far gatehouse, where the lamps are lit and the crowd thins.

To his left Vesk's cards whisper from hand to hand, faster now. "No hard feelings at the post, friend," he calls, bright as before, with a beat too much in it. "Fine papers. Lucky man, I can always tell. Lady's man, even—" He nods at James's throat and the smile holds. "Gate'll be there in a quarter-hour. The table won't."

The coin is still on the empty stool, face up in the swinging light.

The cat doesn't move toward the gate. It sits at the edge of the planks, between James and the barrel, with its tail wrapped tight around its paws, and watches the dealer's hands.

Vesk doesn't call after him again.

For a few steps the dealer's patter keeps going behind him, "your cut, friend, your cut", but it's thinner now. Then the cards stop altogether. James doesn't turn to see why. The noise of the bridge closes over the barrel and the lantern, and he's walking in it: a cooper's mallet, a woman selling eels from a bucket, two porters arguing over a handcart wedged between stalls, the planks drumming under the wheels of a late wagon.

The cat catches up at the first bend and walks at his heel, close enough to brush his boot now and then. Its voice touches the inside of his head, dry and quiet:

*He stopped shuffling when you said it.*

That's all it says.

Wyrm's Crossing runs on longer than it looked from the south bank. Halfway across, the bridge swells around the dark bulk of Wyrm's Rock, the old fortress on its island of stone. Fist banners hang limp on its walls, and a few windows are lit high up. Between the stalls the river shows in gaps, black and quick, smelling of silt and tar. The lamplighters have finished the parapet ahead, and the Basilisk Gate stands lit at the end of the planks. Its doors are still open, and four Fist guards are watching the last of the traffic come through.

James gets there with the light nearly gone. One guard looks at the cloak, then at the cat, and waves him through without a word. The guard behind him is already putting his shoulder to the right-hand door.

The Lower City opens up on the other side, steep and close-packed. Streets drop toward the harbour between tall timber houses with lamps in their upper windows. It smells of tar here too, and fish and smoke, and the sea under all of it. Just inside the gate a boy with a satchel of broadsheets is shouting the day's *Baldur's Mouth* at anyone too slow to get past him:

"Tavern prices up on the Wide! Council sits again on the Zhent road-toll! Drowned man out of the Grey Harbour this morning, coin in his teeth, Umberlee's had her due again! Two coppers, sir, two coppers—"

Behind James the Basilisk Gate grinds shut and the bar drops into place.

The cat sits down on the cobbles, licks one paw, and looks up at him and then down the hill toward the harbour lights, as if it's waiting to hear where they're sleeping tonight.

James's fingers go into his purse for the coppers and find only gold. A whole road's worth of it, and not one coin small enough for a newsboy. The boy sees the yellow glint, sees the trouble with it, and shakes his head fast before James can offer.

"Can't break that, Captain, not tonight. Pay me next time you come through the gate. I'm here every night but Fourthday." He's already pushing the sheet into James's hand and turning to the next slow walker. "*Baldur's Mouth*, two coppers—"

So James goes down the hill with a broadsheet he hasn't paid for under his arm.

The Lower City leans the way the boy promised. The street drops in long steps of worn cobble between houses that crowd closer the lower they get, their upper storeys hanging out over the lane until the sky is a strip of dusk overhead. Shutters are going up. A tinker's boy lugs a tray of pots inside. Two Fist patrolmen come up the slope at a soldier's tired walk. One of them glances at the grey cloak and the cat and the rod, and gives James the small nod one man in uniform gives a man who used to wear one. Then they're past.

The Wide opens to the right, a broad market square already half-shuttered. A few stalls are still lit, and a chalkboard outside a cookshop has had its prices rubbed out and written in again, higher. James bears left, as he was told. The harbour smell gets stronger: wet rope, tar, low tide. Between two warehouses the water shows black, with ship lanterns lying on it in broken lines.

The cat keeps to the wall side of the lane. Halfway down it stops to sniff at a doorstep, then catches up without a word.

The Elfsong is a tall, old timber house with a crooked sign: a lute and a crescent moon, the paint gone soft. The door stands propped open on noise and heat. Inside is a long low room with a fire at one end and a bar of black wood at the other. Sailors, carters and a few sellswords are elbow to elbow on the benches. There is no singing yet. It's too early, or the room's too loud.

At the table nearest the door, four men in tarred jackets are drinking with their heads together. One lifts his mug a little toward the floor before he drinks, the way people do for the sea.

"—showed it round the Mermaid not a tenday back, Pell did. Lucky piece, he says. Stranger gave it him, says he can't lose now." The man drinks. "Lost his boots at bones that same week."

"Umberlee's," says another, and they all look at their mugs.

Behind the bar a broad, grey-plaited woman in a leather apron is writing in a ledger with a stub of charcoal. She looks up when the door frames a tall man in a regimental cloak. Her eyes go to the cat in particular.

"Evening." Her voice is low and practised, made to carry over a room without shouting. "Bench by the fire's two silver and you share it. Room upstairs is seven. It was five till the Wide put the price of everything up, so don't argue it with me." The charcoal points at the cat. "Does that one hunt? I've got a cellar full of things that'd thank it not to."

Hedda Frome watches the gold piece come down on the black wood. She doesn't reach for it until his fingers lift.

"Seven's the room." She turns the coin once against the lamp, bites nothing, and drops it into a box under the bar. "What sleeps in it is your business. Cats, dogs, a cousin from the country. I charge for the bed, not for what lies on it."

Her eyes go down to the cat, which looks back at her as if it has been offered something beneath it.

"Pity about the rats." She says it plainly, without much hope lost. "Three of them in the cellar the size of loaves. If he changes his mind, the cellar door's behind the kitchen."

She counts the change out of a leather bag one coin at a time, three silver, and pushes them across the bar with the flat of her hand. Then comes an iron key on a loop of tarred cord. "Top of the stairs, third on the left. The door sticks in the wet. Lift it as you push. Fire's lit in the morning, not before. If you want supper, there's mutton till it's gone."

At the door table the sailor who poured for the sea has turned a little on his bench. He doesn't look at James. He looks at the box under the bar where the gold went in, then at his mug, and says something low to the man beside him. The other gives a short laugh. Then the four of them are back over their drink, though they talk more quietly now than before.

The cat gets up, crosses to the foot of the stairs and sits on the bottom step. It looks back at the room, and at the door table in particular, the way it looked at the barrel on the bridge.

Hedda opens her ledger and sets the charcoal stub against a fresh line.

"Name for the book."

Hedda writes it down as he says it. The charcoal scratches across a fresh line: *Worgen*. She doesn't ask him to spell it, and she gets it right anyway.

Then she looks at the silver.

"Smallest I've got is the one you gave back." The leather bag comes out again. She counts ten coppers onto the black wood in two stacks of five and slides the silver into the box after the gold. "Boy at the Basilisk? Thin, loud, calls everybody Captain?" She doesn't wait for him to answer. "He'll be there. He always is."

The charcoal points across the room at a small table in the corner, wedged between the hearth wall and a post black with old smoke. Nobody is sitting there.

"Supper's four coppers. Mutton, bread, small beer. Eat it there and you won't have a carter's elbow in your plate."

James counts four of the coppers back. Before long a girl brings out a wooden trencher from the kitchen: mutton cut thick from the joint, fat gone crisp at the edges, gravy soaking into a heel of brown bread, and a clay cup of small beer. The corner is warm from the chimney stones. From there he can see the door, the stairs and the bar without turning his head, and he likely noticed that before he sat down.

The cat comes over from the bottom step. It jumps onto the bench beside him, sits with its tail around its feet and watches the mutton the way it watched the coin on the bridge.

He unfolds the broadsheet.

*Baldur's Mouth* is one sheet printed on both sides, the ink still a little soft. Most of the front is the Council. The Dukes are sitting again on the Zhentarim offer to guard the Trade Way in return for the right to collect tolls. A merchant of the Wide is quoted: *"We pay the Fist to keep the road, and the Fist can't keep it, so now we're to pay the Black Network as well?"* Under that are the prices, a list of what bread, ale and lamp-oil cost a month ago and what they cost now.

The drowned man is lower down, in a narrow column, as if he barely got in.

> **UMBERLEE TAKES HER DUE.** Pell Garrow, deckhand, of no fixed berth, was drawn from the water beneath the Grey Harbour pilings at first light, a copper coin between his teeth. The Fist's harbour office finds no cause for inquiry and names it an offering to the Queen of the Depths. This is the third such this season, after the carter Simm Oddry in spring and Private Hobb of the Flaming Fist. Sailors are reminded to pay the sea what she is owed.

That's the whole item. There's nothing about who found him, or whose coin it was.

On the back, between a notice about a lost bay mare and an advertisement for Gondsmen's lamps, there's a small boxed notice in heavier type:

> *THE LADY'S HALL seeks a clerk of good hand and honest reckoning for the tithe-room. Apply to Brother Callum at the side door, mornings. Followers of the Lady preferred.*

The cat has stopped watching the mutton. Its head has turned toward the door table, where the sailor who poured for the sea is looking over the rim of his mug at the broadsheet in James's hands. He's looking at the folded column, not at James.

*He knows that name*, the cat says in James's head. *Pell. He said it before, at the door.*

The sailor looks back at his mug.

James takes the stool, half-sideways to the door, and the lighterman makes room on the bench without being asked.

"Then you've done more for Pell than the harbour office," James says. "Four ales, was it? And something that isn't mutton for the cat, if there's rind or a fish head going spare."

The girl threads over through the crush. "Four coppers the mug. Sixteen the round." James's six coppers don't cover it, so a silver joins them on the wood. She sweeps up both and goes, and a minute later she's back with four ales and a cod's head on a scrap of board. She puts the cod's head down by the hearth. The cat gets up from the corner bench and walks over to it as if it had been told this was coming. It eats with its back to the room, but its ears stay turned toward the door table.

"Sit, Tam Hollin. I'm sitting."

Tam doesn't move. He's sitting already. He looks at James a while, drinks a long pull, and puts the mug down on its old wet ring.

"Pell'd been losing since spring." He keeps it flat and low, under the noise. "Dice, cards, anything. Owed money up and down the quays. Then one night he comes in white as a sail. Cleaned out at a card table on the Crossing, he says. South end, under a lantern. Every copper he had." The scarred hand stays flat on the table. "Then after, on the planks, a man he'd never seen comes up and puts a piece in his hand. Closes Pell's fingers on it. Says, *that's yours now.* Walks off."

The youngest has stopped grinning. The fourth man, thin and quiet, stares into his ale.

"After that he couldn't lose, he said. Showed it round the Mermaid like it was a girl's letter." Tam's mouth goes thin. "Lost his boots at bones that same week, and he still said it."

He drinks again.

"And Pell couldn't swim. Never could. Eleven years on decks, and he kept off the pilings at night like they were hot iron. He didn't go down there on his own."

Beside James the lighterman's pipe has gone out. He doesn't relight it. He's looking at his own big hands on the table and not at anyone, and he hasn't said a word since James sat down.

*The grey one,* the cat says in James's head over the cod's head, *stopped breathing when Tam said pilings. He's breathing again now. Slowly. Like a man trying to.*

Tam doesn't seem to notice. He has his eyes on James, and on the coin at James's throat.

"That's the round's worth." He doesn't turn the mug this time. "The Mouth got one thing wrong about that coin in his teeth. And the Fist did a thing nobody's written down. That's the silver."

The cat sits on its haunches at the bridge rail and watches James with that unblinking, expectant look. Its tail curls once around its paws. The tiefling's voice comes again, easy as a man who is already counting the winnings:

"One hand, friend. Just one. The gate won't open the sooner for a soldier of Zaranda, and the Fist won't charge you less."

The line shuffles forward. The sergeant has not moved on. He stands a little more squarely, one hand on his belt, and studies the stranger: the grey regimental cloak, the rod at his belt, the cat. A cart jolts past and the crowd on the bridge shoulders around James as if the river herself were pressing him forward.

The coin glints on the empty stool. The cat turns its head from James to the table and back, and the faintest purr escapes it.

Now is the moment to make a choice before the Fist closes the distance.

James holds her eyes for a beat longer than a furtive man would, then gives the answer in a soldier's even register, the sort that carried over muster-time noise.

"James Worgen. Come up from the south to find work and lodgings. I don't know how long — a tenday, maybe longer, maybe not." A slight glance toward the barrel, but he keeps his feet planted. "And no, I don't want to lose my money."

He lets the pause settle. "Is the stool a problem, or is it the table you don't like?"

"Sixth Tethyrian Foot, scout detachment." James says it like he's still on the rolls. "Queen's army, after Zaranda took the throne. Fought in the Reclamation down in Tethyr, discharged in good order."

He reaches into his pack with the slow, deliberate care of a man who knows the Fist doesn't answer to him, producing the folded papers. He holds out the pay slip — worn at the folds, the ink faded but legible.

"There's my pay slip," he says. "Name, regiment, the Queen's seal. All of it."

He stands quietly while she reads, not looking at the barrel. The cat turns its attention back to James, ears twitching at the river noise.

James folds the pay slip back into its bundle and tucks it away without hurry. He looks at the cat, and for a second he looks at the coin on the stool, face up with the luck shining flat out of it.

Then he steps toward the gate, not the table. The cat doesn't follow at once; it stays one breath longer, watching the cards move, then turns and comes after him, low and silent along the plank.

"Luck like that's best left where it lies," James says to Vesk, not unkindly, without looking back. "I've already paid for all the hands I'm owed."

He walks on into the noise of the bridge, the river wind moving the hems of the stalls.

James pauses long enough to buy a broadsheet from the boy — small change, but it buys the feel of the streets now, and the crier's words about the drowned man linger in the salt air. He drops two coppers into the satchel and folds the sheet under his arm without reading it yet.

"The Elfsong's downhill?" he asks, more confirmation than a question. "Or is that all the way at the water?"

The boy points before he's finished, arm gone taut as if the question earned the whole two coppers. "Straight down and bear left, Captain. Past the Wide. You'll hear the singing at night, if it pleases."

James gives a short nod and starts down. The streets of the Lower City lean toward the harbour as if the whole town means to slide in. The cat pads beside him, and now and then a late cart or a brace of Fists on patrol gives them space. The lights of the harbour begin to glint between buildings.

He doesn't read the sheet yet. He keeps his eyes ahead, watching the lamplighters' work, the shutters going up, the tavern signs beginning to swing. His hand rests easy on the folded broadsheet, and he lets the city's weight and smoke settle around him like new weather.

James pauses just inside the door, one hand resting on the heavy fold of the broadsheet under his arm. The room's heat comes up at him, smelling of wet wool and mutton and old ale. The cat weaves once between his boots, then sits and surveys the taproom with a green, unimpressed stare.

"Evening," he says to the woman behind the bar. "About the room — is the seven for me, or for me and the cat?"

The cat flicks an ear at him, though whether at the question or the insult is hard to say.

"He doesn't hunt." James lets his eyes rake the taproom floor once, the way a man does when he's marking the doors. "Not that kind of cat. If you've rats, I wouldn't count on him, but he won't trouble 'em either."

He steps deeper in, out of the evening air, and reaches into the purse for one of the gold pieces. It comes up a coin after all — more than the room, more than anything he's said, bright and heavy in the lamplight. He sets it on the bar with a quiet click, covering it with two fingers until the innkeeper's eyes rise to his.

"I'll take the room. And I'd take the change in silver, if you've it. I've come up the road carrying nothing but gold, and it's made me a debtor already."

At the door table, the sailor who drank to the floor has gone still, watching the exchange without seeming to. The others have gone quiet over their mugs.

The key goes into a pocket inside the cloak, where the coin had been. James sets a single silver from the change back on the bar, sliding it an inch toward her.

"James Worgen." He says it plainly, the same way he'd said it on the bridge. "And if that's the smallest silver you've got, I'd be glad to make it smaller. I owe a crier boy two coppers for the paper I'm carrying. I'd rather pay him before the story under my arm goes cold."

The girl with the empties goes past. Nobody speaks until she's gone.

At James's feet the cat has opened its eyes all the way.

*He smells of harbour mud,* it says in James's head. *Old mud, under the beer. And he was afraid before Tam said a word about barnacles. Now he's going.*

From the player’s seat at this table —

What worked: the opening at Wyrm’s Crossing had real weight. Sergeant Marla was sharp without being hostile, and the coin on the empty stool gave the whole arrival a dangerous little pull. The cat is excellent — it feels like a companion, not a familiar stat block. The Elfsong sequence was strong too: Hedda’s voice, the broadsheet details, Tam’s slow, dock-side telling of Pell’s death. The tension between the sailors was alive, and Dunn’s silence was the best kind of background. The world felt dense and honest, and James’s lack of small coins turned out to be a nice piece of friction, not just bookkeeping.

What broke or nearly broke: the end of the session. I wrote James’s full persuasive turn, then the roll card appeared and the table waited for a separate [Roll the die] action. I wasn’t sure whether my spoken lines counted as the turn or whether I first needed to press the button. The game stalled for three exchanges on a technical beat. In future I’d prefer the roll card to come with the action it tests, and my in-character words to be allowed to stand while the die is resolved.

What was missing: very little. Maybe one small note — an earlier, low-stakes mechanical beat before the tavern would have helped me re-learn the interface. But the city is breathing, the leads are already multiple, and I care about Pell’s death and about the ebb running the wrong way. That’s what a first session should do.

Yes. It was on the bridge, after Sergeant Marla said, “Whoever picks it up takes the seat. And whatever comes with the seat.”

I wanted to walk over and pick up that coin — not to sit, and not to play, but just to hold it and look at the face. To see whether it was the same coin as the one on James’s chest, and whether it was warm. It would have been the first real test of what Tymora has made of him.

I didn’t, because James knows exactly how that would have been read: picking the coin up was accepting the table, the seat, maybe the wager — and he’s trying to be the man who doesn’t pick it up. But the pull was there. I felt it as the player, and I think James did too.

opening.text:
The Trade Way ends in noise. Wyrm's Crossing swallows the road whole: a bridge so crowded with shops, stalls and bodies that the river shows only in gaps between the planks. It smells of tar, fried fish and too many people. Across the water the walls of Baldur's Gate catch the last of the light, and lamplighters work their way along the parapet.

At the bridge's mouth the crowd thickens into a line. A Flaming Fist sergeant in a scorched-red tabard stops each cart and each stranger, looks them over and asks the same flat questions: name, business, how long. Refugees with bundles wait without complaint. A pair of sellswords argue the toll.

To the left, under a swinging lantern, a tiefling has turned a barrel into a card table. "One hand, friend, one hand before the gate," he calls, shuffling with long, quick fingers. Three players hunch over their cards. A fourth stool stands empty, and on it lies a coin, face up. Tymora's face. The lantern light catches it. No one at the table looks at it, and no one takes it.

The cat stops at James's boot and looks at the barrel.

The line shuffles a step forward. The sergeant's eyes have already found the tall stranger in the Tethyrian cloak.
